title: Forty subjects
hookLine: a newcomer is handed one verse as a test; his answer becomes a book with forty ways to meditate
tomorrow: how you sweep a floor might show which one suits you. how?

cards: Some job interviews skip the résumé and slide one problem across the table: solve this. Tradition says that's how Buddhaghosa was welcomed at the Great Monastery in Sri Lanka.
The senior monks gave the newcomer a single verse. It asks: there's a tangle inside and a tangle outside, and people are caught in it; who can untangle this tangle?
His answer grew into a whole book, the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification. And the story adds a twist. The gods hid his manuscript, and he wrote it again.
They hid it a second time, and he wrote it a third. When all three copies were laid side by side, they matched word for word.

teach.b: Deep inside that book is a list, and it answers last week's question: which way in is yours? The word is kammatthana, a meditation subject, the thing you work with when you sit. Buddhaghosa lists forty.
Ten kasinas: discs of earth, water, fire, wind, colors and light to gaze at. Ten kinds of foulness, the body after death.
Ten recollections: the Buddha, the teaching, the community, generosity, death, the breath, and more. Four divine abodes: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity. Four formless states.
One perception, of food. One defining, of the elements of the body. Forty.
And here's the surprise: this isn't a menu where every dish suits everyone. Some subjects fit some people and not others, and Buddhaghosa spends pages on how to match them.
Only a couple he calls useful for everyone, like loving-kindness and remembering death. So the answer to which one is yours is: the one that fits you.
Same house, forty doors. A door that's wrong for you may be exactly right for the person beside you.

how: In Theravada practice the Visuddhimagga is studied as a guide to meditation; a teacher may give a student one subject, such as the breath or loving-kindness, and add others over time.

games.q: your roommate downloads a meditation app and tries a different kind every night for a month, never the same twice. what would Buddhaghosa say?
o: find the one that fits you and stay with it; forty doors, one at a time.
great plan: sampling everything is how you make the fastest progress.
skip all the options; only the breath counts as real meditation.
games.why: the list is wide on purpose, but it's for matching, not sampling. you go in by the door that fits, and you keep going.

practice: Read the list slowly as it comes up on the screen, one group at a time: discs, foulness, recollections, divine abodes, formless states, food, elements. Don't choose anything.
Just notice which door you lean toward and which you lean away from, and let both be information.

wordCard.voice: Kammatthana: a meditation subject, the thing you work with in meditation. Buddhaghosa lists forty of them.

orig.note: Pali: meditation subject, the object or theme a meditator works with.

carryVoice: Carry this: forty doors, one house, and no door wrong for everyone. That's day one of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga III.104–105 (the forty meditation subjects: ten kasinas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abodes, four immaterial states, one perception, one defining)
Visuddhimagga III.57–58 (the generally useful subjects: loving-kindness and mindfulness of death)
Samyutta Nikaya 1.23 (the tangle verse) and Culavamsa 37 (Buddhaghosa's test and the three copies)
